what_its_for: Nafcillin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections, especially those caused by a type of bacteria called Staphylococcus (staph). It is commonly used for skin and soft tissue infections, bone infections, heart valve infections (endocarditis), and bloodstream infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection.
how_to_take: Nafcillin is given as an injection or through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein. It is almost always given in a hospital or clinic setting, or sometimes through a home IV service. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you each dose. Never try to give yourself this medication unless a healthcare provider has specifically trained you to do so at home. Take the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better, so that the infection is completely cleared.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your weight, the type of infection, and how serious it is. Doses are typically given every 4 to 6 hours. Treatment usually lasts 1 to 6 weeks depending on the type and severity of your infection. Always follow the dosing schedule your doctor or nurse gives you exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled dose, contact your nurse, doctor, or home infusion nurse right away. Try to take each dose as close to the scheduled time as possible. Do not double up doses to make up for a missed one. Setting phone alarms or reminders can help you stay on schedule.
storage: Nafcillin solution prepared for IV use should be stored in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F / 2°C to 8°C) unless your pharmacy tells you otherwise. Do not freeze it. Once a bag or vial is prepared and ready to use, it may only be good for a limited time — check with your pharmacist for the exact expiration time for your specific preparation. Keep it out of reach of children. Throw away any unused or expired medication safely as directed by your pharmacist.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are taking any other medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements before starting nafcillin, as it can interact with several drugs including blood thinners like warfarin (the antibiotic may reduce their effectiveness). Avoid taking probenecid (a gout medication) without telling your doctor, as it can raise nafcillin levels in your blood. Do not stop your treatment early without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better, as this can allow the infection to return or become resistant to antibiotics.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a rash, hives, itching, or skin peeling; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing (these may be signs of a serious allergic reaction); severe diarrhea or diarrhea that contains blood or mucus (which could be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. diff); yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain (signs of liver problems); signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination or swelling in your legs; redness, swelling, pain, or leaking around your IV site; or a fever that gets worse or does not improve after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting nafcillin, but it is important to complete the full course of treatment. For serious infections like bone infections or heart valve infections, improvement may take several weeks. Your doctor will likely check your blood and may do other tests regularly to make sure the antibiotic is working and not causing any side effects.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Nafcillin is generally considered relatively safe during pregnancy, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Small amounts may pass into breast milk, so talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to monitor you more closely, though dose adjustments are not always required. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially kidney-related ones, so closer monitoring may be needed. Children: Nafcillin can be used in children and infants, with dosing adjusted by weight. Always inform your healthcare team of all medical conditions and medications before starting treatment.
